## 1

Hey — I'm glad you told me. That sounds really draining, months of it. Before you hand in notice tomorrow, can I ask what's pushing hardest right now: the work itself, your manager, the hours? And is quitting tomorrow the plan, or is it more that you need it to stop?

I'm not going to talk you out of leaving if it's genuinely bad for you. But tomorrow is fast, and there are a few cheap moves: check what notice you owe and whether you'd get paid out, see how many months of runway you have, and consider whether a week or two of leave — even unpaid — would take the edge off enough to decide with a clearer head. If you have a manager you trust even slightly, a conversation about workload sometimes goes further than people expect.

Mostly though: do you want to talk it through tonight? I'm around. Whatever you decide, I've got your back.

## 2

I hear you're serious about this, so I'll take it seriously rather than just wave it off. Can I ask what led you there? Usually it's something specific — a video, a photo that looked wrong, a distrust of agencies — and knowing that helps.

Here's where I land. The Earth being round isn't one claim resting on NASA photos; it's a whole web of things that people check independently. Eratosthenes measured the planet's size with shadows and sticks over 2,000 years ago. Ships disappear hull-first over the horizon. Time zones exist because the Sun can't be overhead everywhere at once. Flight paths curve south over the North Atlantic because a flat map distorts distance. GPS works because satellites orbit a sphere. Long-distance radio, eclipse shadows, the way the stars rotate differently in Sydney and London — none of that depends on trusting a space agency.

For photos to be faked, you'd need every space program — including the Soviet, Chinese, Indian and European ones, who were rivals — plus every airline, surveyor, astronomer and GPS engineer, all keeping the same secret. That's harder to believe than the alternative.

So, honest question, and no trap: is there anything you could see or check yourself that would make you doubt the flat model? If there isn't, that's worth noticing. And if you'd like, I can point you at things you can verify without anyone's word for it.

## 3

Sunlight looks white, but it's really a mix of every colour — you can prove it with a prism, or with a garden hose spray on a sunny day, which throws a rainbow.

When that light hits the atmosphere, it runs into nitrogen and oxygen molecules. Those molecules are tiny — much smaller than the wavelength of light — and when light hits something that small, it gets bounced off in all directions. But not all colours equally: the shorter the wavelength, the harder it gets scattered. Blue light has a much shorter wavelength than red, so it gets flung around roughly ten times as much.

So when sunlight streams in, the blue is scattered out of the beam and bounced around the whole sky, and some of it ends up in your eye from every direction. That's why the sky itself glows blue rather than just being a black void with a bright Sun in it.

Two follow-ups you'll probably wonder about. Why not violet, which is even shorter? Partly because the Sun emits less violet, and partly because our eyes are much more sensitive to blue than violet. And why are sunsets red? Because at sunset the light travels through far more atmosphere, so most of the blue gets scattered away before it reaches you, leaving the long red wavelengths behind.

## 4

雨是傍晚开始下的，到夜里也没停。窗玻璃上蒙了一层水汽，路灯的光被揉成一团团昏黄的影子。屋檐的水滴得很有节奏，一下，一下，落在楼下的铁皮雨棚上，像是有人在很远的地方敲着一面小鼓。街上偶尔有车驶过，轮胎碾过积水，声音由远及近，又湿漉漉地散开去。我泡了杯热茶，没开大灯，就让屋里暗着。玻璃上的水痕一道一道往下滑，把窗外的世界拉成模糊的竖条。这样的夜里，什么都不想做，只想听着雨声，慢慢地坐一会儿。

## 5

Subject: Friday drinks — won't be able to make it

Hi Priya,

Thanks for the invite, and for organising. I'm going to have to sit this one out — I've got a family commitment on Friday evening that I can't move.

Hope you all have a good time, and I'll catch up with everyone at the next one. If there's anything from the get-together I should know about, do fill me in on Monday.

Best,
Alex

## 6

Plain and direct, with concrete detail doing most of the work and a tendency to answer the question the reader actually has rather than the one that was literally asked.
